programs.name: Statewide Medicaid Managed Care (SMMC) Long-Term Care Program
programs.tagline: Medicaid-covered home care services to keep your loved one out of nursing home placement
programs.intro:
If your loved one needs nursing home-level care but wants to stay home, Florida's SMMC-LTC waivers provide comprehensive home and community-based services through Medicaid. This includes adult day health care, attendant care, respite care, and case management, all designed to prevent nursing home placement.

Your loved one must qualify medically (a CARES assessment confirming Nursing Facility Level of Care) and financially (income under $2,982/month for a single applicant, countable assets under $2,000 in 2026). Because this program consolidates several former waivers (Alzheimer's Disease, Nursing Home Diversion, Assisted Living for the Elderly, and Consumer Directed Care Plus), there is a statewide waitlist with a priority score from 1 to 7.

Unlike nursing home Medicaid, which cannot have a waitlist, eligible applicants for home care are placed on a waiting list and prioritized by frailty. Families should apply early, even if immediate services aren't needed. If income exceeds the limit, a Qualified Income Trust (Miller Trust) is a standard legal workaround used by thousands of Floridians.

applicationGuide.summary: Three agencies, one journey. Start with your local Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC) for a waitlist screening; DOEA runs the medical CARES assessment; DCF handles the financial side; AHCA oversees the health plan you choose once you're enrolled.

steps.title: Call your local ADRC for a waitlist screening
steps.description: Call the statewide Elder Helpline at 1-800-963-5337 (1-800-963-5337). They route you to the Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC) for your county. The ADRC does a telephonic screening that assigns a priority score from 1 to 7 based on frailty. Scores of 4 or higher (or 'imminent risk' at 7) are released from the waitlist faster.

steps.title: Complete the CARES assessment
steps.description: Once released from the waitlist, the Department of Elder Affairs (DOEA) sends a CARES nurse or social worker to your loved one's home for an in-person clinical evaluation. This confirms Nursing Facility Level of Care (NFLOC) eligibility.

steps.title: Get AHCA Form 5000-3008 signed by the primary care physician
steps.description: This medical certification is a gatekeeper document: the application cannot proceed without a signed Form 3008 from your loved one's doctor.

steps.title: Apply for financial eligibility through DCF
steps.description: Apply through the Department of Children and Families (DCF) via the ACCESS Florida portal. The 2026 income limit is $2,982/month for a single applicant. If income exceeds the limit, a Qualified Income Trust (Miller Trust) must be in place before DCF can approve.

steps.title: Select a managed care plan
steps.description: Once medical and financial approvals are final, Florida Medicaid Choice Counseling will send a letter asking you to select a health plan (Sunshine Health, Humana, UnitedHealthcare, or similar). The plan is what actually delivers the home health aides, respite care, and adult day services.

applicationGuide.processingTime: Highly variable, depending on waitlist position and priority score. Higher-scoring applicants move through faster.
applicationGuide.waitlist: The screening gives a priority score. A score of 30 or higher goes on the wait list. A score under 30 is not placed on the wait list at all, and Florida mails information about other community programs instead. Releases happen monthly by score and frailty, not by how long someone has waited. After release there is a medical form that must be returned within 30 days.
applicationGuide.tip: Apply early even if services aren't needed immediately. The waitlist uses a priority score system, so being in the queue matters even before urgent need hits.

documentsNeeded: Their Medicaid number, if they already have one. The screener also asks for a Social Security number, but the form says giving it is voluntary.
Monthly income and roughly how much is in savings, for your loved one and their spouse if married. You can decline to answer.
A list of daily tasks they need help with, such as bathing, dressing, eating, using the bathroom, and walking. Also any memory loss or dementia diagnosis, and who helps now.
Nothing needs to be mailed or shown. The whole first step is a phone conversation that takes about 45 minutes to an hour.

Income over $2,982/month may still qualify through a Qualified Income Trust (Miller Trust). This legal workaround is standard in Florida and is used by thousands of applicants; without it, being even $1 over results in denial.

contentSections.text: How the waitlist works: your local ADRC screens applicants by phone and assigns a priority score from 1 (lowest need) to 7 (imminent risk). Scores of 4 or higher are released from the waitlist first. Applying early matters because the score-based queue rewards being in line before urgent need hits.

Over the income limit? A Qualified Income Trust (Miller Trust) is a standard Florida workaround. If gross income exceeds $2,982/month, the excess can be legally funneled through the trust so your loved one still qualifies. Without a Miller Trust in place, being even $1 over the limit results in denial.

Community Spouse Protection: if one spouse applies while the other stays at home, the at-home spouse can keep up to $162,660 in assets in 2026 (the Community Spouse Resource Allowance). This is a major relief for families worried about depleting all savings to qualify one spouse.

60-month look-back is strictly enforced. Any assets gifted or sold for less than fair market value in the 5 years before applying trigger a penalty period. 2026 penalty divisor is $10,645: every $10,645 given away equals one month of Medicaid ineligibility. Plan early with an elder-law attorney if gifting is being considered.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house if it's worth more than $2,000?
faqs.answer: Yes. The primary home is exempt from the $2,000 asset limit if your loved one lives there or has intent to return. Home equity cap is $752,000 in 2026 for a single applicant; if a spouse or dependent child lives in the home, the equity cap is waived entirely.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is $3,200/month, just over the limit?
faqs.answer: They can still qualify. Florida's income cap is $2,982/month in 2026, but a Qualified Income Trust (Miller Trust) is a standard legal tool that lets applicants over the limit funnel excess income through the trust and still qualify. Without it, even being $1 over results in denial. An elder-law attorney can set one up quickly.

faqs.question: How long is the waitlist?
faqs.answer: It varies by region and priority score. The ADRC screening assigns a score from 1 to 7 based on frailty, and those at 'imminent risk' (7) or with the highest care needs (4+) are released from the waitlist first. Apply early: the ranking rewards being in line before urgent need hits.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes. You'll need a Durable Power of Attorney (DPOA), a Legal Guardianship order, or to be designated as an Authorized Representative on the DCF ACCESS Florida portal. Without one of these, the agencies can't share information or take direction from you.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one gave away money to qualify for Medicaid?
faqs.answer: Florida strictly enforces a 60-month look-back. Any gifts or below-fair-market-value transfers in the 5 years before applying trigger a penalty period. The 2026 penalty divisor is $10,645: every $10,645 given away equals one month of ineligibility. Plan with an elder-law attorney before gifting if Medicaid is on the horizon.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get both this program and nursing home Medicaid?
faqs.answer: No. SMMC-LTC (home and community services) and ICP (nursing home Medicaid) are alternatives, not both-at-once. The financial eligibility rules are the same, but a person is enrolled in one or the other based on whether they're living at home or in a facility.

faqs.question: What do DOEA, DCF, and AHCA actually do in this process?
faqs.answer: Three different agencies, three different jobs. DOEA (Department of Elder Affairs) runs the CARES assessment that confirms your loved one needs nursing-home level care. DCF (Department of Children and Families) handles the financial eligibility review through ACCESS Florida. AHCA (Agency for Health Care Administration) oversees the managed care health plans once your loved one is enrolled. Most caregivers start at the ADRC, which coordinates the first handoff.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's care needs change after they're enrolled?
faqs.answer: Reassessments happen annually (every 12 months) and any time there's a significant change in condition. The assigned managed care plan is required to adjust services based on reassessment results. Call your plan's case manager as soon as needs shift.

programs.name: Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE)
programs.tagline: All-inclusive medical care for your loved one if they need nursing home level care but want to stay home.

localEntities.name: Check AHCA for the full list of 30+ participating counties

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 55+ and needs nursing home level care but wants to stay at home, PACE provides everything under one program, doctors, nurses, medications, transportation, meals, and even adult day care. Because PACE covers all medical care through one coordinated team, your loved one won't need to manage separate Medicare providers or coordinate between different specialists.

PACE is now available in more than 30 Florida counties, including the Tampa Bay area, Orlando, Jacksonville, South Florida, and the Panhandle. Your loved one must qualify for nursing home level care but be able to live safely in the community with PACE services. Most participants have both Medicare and Medicaid, though PACE helps with Medicaid enrollment if needed.

The program covers everything at no additional cost beyond Medicare/Medicaid: primary care, specialists, prescription drugs, hospital stays, home care, adult day health care, meals, and transportation to medical appointments. Average participants are 76 years old with complex medical needs.

Who it's for: the program works best for seniors with complex medical needs who require significant daily help and want to avoid nursing home placement.

Private pay and Medicaid planning: if your loved one doesn't initially qualify for Medicaid, they can enroll as a private-pay participant while the PACE team assists with 2026 Medicaid planning strategies (including Qualified Income Trust setup) to meet eligibility.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their current doctor if they enroll in PACE?
faqs.answer: No, your loved one must receive all care through the PACE team. Because PACE provides comprehensive coordinated care, participants cannot see outside providers except in emergencies. The PACE center assigns a primary care physician and care team.

faqs.question: What if my loved one lives outside the major metro areas?
faqs.answer: PACE has expanded significantly and is now available in more than 30 Florida counties, including the Tampa Bay area, Orlando, Jacksonville, and Southwest Florida. If PACE is not yet available in your loved one's specific zip code, check with AHCA or consider the Statewide Medicaid Managed Care Long-Term Care program as an alternative.

faqs.question: Can my loved one disenroll from PACE if they don't like it?
faqs.answer: Yes, PACE enrollment is voluntary and your loved one can disenroll at any time. They would return to regular Medicare and Medicaid coverage and regain the ability to choose their own doctors and services.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one needs to move to a nursing home permanently?
faqs.answer: PACE covers nursing facility care when needed. If your loved one requires permanent nursing home placement, PACE coordinates and pays for that care. The goal is always to help participants return home when possible.

faqs.question: How much does my family pay out-of-pocket for PACE services?
faqs.answer: If your loved one has both Medicare and Medicaid, there are no out-of-pocket costs. Medicare-only participants pay a monthly premium for long-term care services. PACE covers everything else, no copays, deductibles, or additional charges.

faqs.question: Can I apply for PACE while my loved one is in the hospital?
faqs.answer: Yes, hospital discharge planners often initiate PACE enrollment for patients who need nursing home level care but want to return home. The enrollment process can begin before discharge, though the in-home assessments happen after your loved one returns home.

faqs.question: What if my loved one doesn't have Medicaid but their income is too high to qualify?
faqs.answer: PACE enrollment specialists help with Medicaid planning strategies. The 2026 gross monthly income limit is $2,982 (300% of the Federal Benefit Rate). If your loved one exceeds this, they may still qualify by establishing a Qualified Income Trust (Miller Trust), or through spend-down processes that account for medical expenses.

faqs.question: Does PACE provide transportation to non-medical appointments like grocery shopping?
faqs.answer: PACE primarily provides transportation to medical appointments, adult day health care, and the PACE center. Transportation for other needs like shopping is typically arranged through the home care services or community partnerships, but varies by provider.

programs.name: Medicaid Medicare Savings Programs (QMB, SLMB, QI)
programs.tagline: If your loved one is on Medicare with a limited income, they may qualify for Florida programs that pay their $202.90 monthly Part B premiums, plus deductibles and copays.
programs.intro:
If you're looking for a way to ease the financial pressure on your loved one, Florida's Medicare Savings Programs can be a true lifesaver. For 2026, these programs can stop the $202.90 monthly Part B premium from being taken out of their Social Security check, putting over $2,400 back in their pocket annually. Depending on their income, they might even qualify for the QMB level, which covers almost all out-of-pocket medical costs — meaning doctors can no longer bill them for Medicare deductibles or copays.

Enrolling is one of the kindest things you can do to protect their health and savings. Beyond the premium relief, qualifying for any of these programs automatically triggers "Extra Help" with prescription costs, which can save them thousands more at the pharmacy. As long as your loved one is a Florida resident with Medicare Part A and meets certain income and asset limits (their home and one car typically won't count), this support is waiting for them. It's a wonderful way to ensure they get the care they deserve without the constant worry of medical bills.

contentSections.title: Program Tiers: QMB vs SLMB vs QI
contentSections.content: QMB (Qualified Medicare Beneficiary) covers the most but has the lowest income limit ($1,350/month individual). Pays Medicare Part B premiums, all deductibles, and copays. SLMB (Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary) covers only Part B premiums for slightly higher incomes. QI (Qualifying Individual) also covers Part B premiums but operates on limited annual funding, first-come, first-served until money runs out.

faqs.question: Can I apply for all three programs at the same time?
faqs.answer: No, these are income-tiered programs. Florida will automatically place your loved one in the program they qualify for based on income. If income is too high for QMB, they'll be considered for SLMB, then QI.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income is $50 over the limit?
faqs.answer: Income limits are strict, but Florida applies a $20 general exclusion to unearned income first. Also, income limits change every April 1 based on federal poverty levels, so your loved one might qualify later in the year.

faqs.question: My loved one got a bill from their doctor even though they have QMB, is this right?
faqs.answer: No. Providers are prohibited from billing QMB beneficiaries for Medicare deductibles or coinsurance. Contact the provider's billing department immediately and show them your loved one's QMB card. If problems persist, call 1-877-411-6810.

faqs.question: How is household size determined for the income limits?
faqs.answer: Florida counts all blood relatives or spouses who rely on your loved one for at least half their financial support. This can include adult children or grandchildren living in the home, not just spouses.

faqs.question: Does my loved one's house count toward the asset limit?
faqs.answer: No, the primary residence is exempt regardless of value. The asset limits only apply to countable resources like savings accounts, investments, and additional properties.

faqs.question: If my loved one qualifies for QI this year, are they guaranteed coverage next year?
faqs.answer: No. QI operates on annual funding that can run out. Your loved one must reapply each year, and approvals are first-come, first-served. Apply early in January for the best chance.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can apply as authorized representatives. You'll need legal documentation showing you can act on your loved one's behalf, such as power of attorney or guardianship papers.

faqs.question: What's the difference between QMB and regular Florida Medicaid?
faqs.answer: QMB specifically helps with Medicare costs and has different eligibility rules. Your loved one can have QMB and regular Medicaid simultaneously, or just QMB if their income is too high for full Medicaid but low enough for Medicare cost-sharing help.

programs.name: SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program)
programs.tagline: Up to $298/month for groceries if your loved one is 60+ on a fixed income

localEntities.name: Local DCF service centers statewide (search by ZIP inside the MyACCESS Portal: myaccess.myflfamilies.com)

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 60+ and struggling with grocery costs, SNAP provides monthly benefits loaded onto an EBT card for food purchases. Maximum benefit: $298/month for a single person, $546 for two people.

Florida uses a senior-friendly income test: the gross limit is 200% of the federal poverty level ($2,610/month for one person in 2026), nearly double the 130% limit most states apply to working-age households. On top of that, reporting medical expenses above $35/month, Medicare premiums, prescriptions, out-of-pocket costs, lowers the 'countable income' used to calculate the actual benefit.

The program covers fruits, vegetables, meat, dairy, and grains. As of April 20, 2026, Florida's Healthy SNAP rules also prohibit soda, energy drinks, candy, and ultra-processed shelf-stable desserts. Benefits are calculated as the maximum allotment minus 30% of net income, a single senior with $800/month net income receives $298 − $240 = $58/month.

contentSections.text: Applicants 60+ can use Florida's Elderly Simplified Application Project (ESAP), a shorter application, 36-month certification (vs. 12 months), and no in-person interview required. Ask DCF about ESAP when you apply.

How the benefit amount is calculated: maximum allotment for the household size minus 30% of net income. Example: a single senior with $800/month net income receives $298 − $240 = $58/month. Reporting medical expenses above $35/month lowers net income and raises the monthly benefit.

Effective April 20, 2026: Florida's Healthy SNAP rules prohibit using benefits for soda, energy drinks (65mg+ caffeine per 8oz), candy, and ultra-processed shelf-stable desserts. Sports drinks (Gatorade, Powerade), sparkling water (LaCroix, Bubly), and drinks with >50% juice or <5g added sugar per serving are still allowed. Full list at healthysnap.myflfamilies.com.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep SNAP if they live in my house but don't pay rent?
faqs.answer: Yes, if they buy and prepare food separately from your household, they can apply as a one-person household. Paying zero rent means no shelter deduction, but taking responsibility for even one utility bill (like a cell phone) restores part of it. Their share of the home isn't a problem, the primary residence is an excluded asset.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's Social Security is $1,400/month, too high for the income limit?
faqs.answer: It's not too high. Florida uses 200% of the federal poverty level ($2,610/month for one person in 2026) as the gross income limit for senior/disabled households, nearly double the 130% threshold most states use. Medical expenses above $35/month further lower their countable income, which raises the monthly benefit.

faqs.question: Can I apply for SNAP on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can act as their Authorized Representative. Your loved one signs a form designating you, and you handle the application and any interview. They should still be available by phone during the eligibility interview, but you can lead the conversation. For applicants 60+ using ESAP, the interview is often waived entirely.

faqs.question: How does owning a house affect SNAP eligibility?
faqs.answer: It doesn't. The primary residence is an excluded asset regardless of value, it never counts toward the $4,500 limit. Rental property or a second home is counted. Property taxes and homeowner's insurance can be deducted as shelter costs, lowering countable income.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income changes after approval?
faqs.answer: Florida uses Simplified Reporting for most senior households. You only need to notify DCF if monthly income crosses $1,696 (130% FPL for one person). If it does, report within 10 days of the following month to avoid overpayments you'd later have to repay. Reporting income decreases or new medical expenses is always optional, and often increases benefits.

faqs.question: Can my loved one use SNAP and still get meals from a senior center?
faqs.answer: Yes, congregate meals at senior centers and Meals on Wheels don't count against SNAP. The programs are designed to work together. SNAP covers groceries at the store; senior center meals fill social gaps.

faqs.question: What can't my loved one buy with SNAP anymore in Florida?
faqs.answer: As of April 20, 2026, SNAP in Florida can no longer be used for soda, energy drinks with 65mg+ caffeine per 8oz, candy, or ultra-processed shelf-stable desserts. Sports drinks, sparkling waters, and beverages with more than 50% juice or fewer than 5g of added sugar per serving are still eligible. Full rules at healthysnap.myflfamilies.com.

programs.name: LIHEAP (Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program)
programs.tagline: Get help with your energy bill toward your loved one's electric and gas bills if household income is under $2,679/month for one person.
programs.intro:
If your loved one struggles with high electric or gas bills, LIHEAP provides a one-time payment set by your county, generally $200 to $700 for heating or cooling help directly to their utility company. Year-round crisis help is capped at $1,000 per household per program year, resetting each October 1 for those in a crisis, such as facing disconnection. The payment amount depends on household income, size, and whether they need heating or cooling assistance.

Your loved one qualifies if their gross household income is at or below $2,679/month for one person, $3,504 for two people, or higher limits for larger households. They automatically qualify if they already receive SNAP, SSI, or TANF. LIHEAP is active in all 67 Florida counties; you apply through the agency designated for your loved one's specific county. Heating assistance generally runs through March 31, and cooling assistance opens April 1.

The program prioritizes households with seniors 60+, children under 5, or disabled members. Because funding is limited, applications often pause when money runs out, so apply as early as possible when the program opens.

faqs.answer: Your loved one can still apply, but they'll need additional documentation like a lease agreement showing they're responsible for utilities. The household must be responsible for paying the heating or cooling bills, even if the account isn't in their name.

faqs.question: Where do I find the right LIHEAP provider for my loved one's county?
faqs.answer: LIHEAP is active in all 67 Florida counties. To find the specific local provider for your loved one's area, call 2-1-1, use the state assistance line at 850-717-8450, or check the directory at FloridaJobs.org/LIHEAP. If funding for the season has run out at their local agency, 2-1-1 can also identify other local utility assistance programs.

faqs.question: How much will my loved one actually receive?
faqs.answer: Heating and cooling awards generally run $200 to $700, and year-round crisis help is capped at $1,000 per program year. Amounts vary by county and available funding. The exact amount depends on household income, size, fuel type, and whether it's for heating or cooling. The payment goes directly to the utility company, not to your loved one.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get LIHEAP if they're already receiving SNAP or SSI?
faqs.answer: Yes, receiving SNAP, SSI, or TANF actually makes your loved one automatically eligible for LIHEAP without having to meet the income limits separately. Just bring their benefits award letter as proof of eligibility.

faqs.question: What happens if applications are closed when we try to apply?
faqs.answer: LIHEAP funding is limited and applications often pause when money runs out, especially during peak summer and winter months. Call your county provider to ask when applications will reopen or to be placed on a waiting list for the next funding cycle.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can help with the application process. You'll need all the required documents and information about your loved one's household. Some counties may require your loved one to sign the application or speak with a caseworker directly for verification.

faqs.question: How often can my loved one receive LIHEAP assistance?
faqs.answer: Most counties allow one payment per heating season and one per cooling season per year. However, if your loved one faces a utility emergency with disconnection notice, they may qualify for crisis assistance, capped at $1,000 per program year.

faqs.question: Does my loved one's house or car count against the income limits?
faqs.answer: No, LIHEAP has no asset limits. Your loved one's home, car, savings accounts, or other assets don't count against eligibility, only monthly income matters for qualification.

programs.name: EHEAP (Emergency Home Energy Assistance for the Elderly Program)
programs.tagline: Emergency help for households with someone 60 or older when heating or cooling fails, including repair or replacement of the equipment.
programs.intro:
If your loved one is 60 or older and their home has become dangerously hot or cold, EHEAP is the program built for that moment. It helps low-income Florida households with at least one person age 60 or older who are facing a home energy emergency, and it is administered through Area Agencies on Aging and local Aging and Disability Resource Centers rather than the county agency that handles regular utility assistance.

The important difference from LIHEAP is what the money can do. LIHEAP pays down a utility bill. EHEAP responds to the emergency itself, and its described uses include repairs or replacement of existing heating and cooling equipment, not only the bill. Some regions also provide fans, portable units, blankets, or space heaters. A household can qualify for a benefit in each season, and the cooling season runs April 1 through September 30 while the heating season runs October 1 through March 31.

Eligibility rests on three things: someone in the home is 60 or older, the household income is at or below 60 percent of Florida's State Median Income, and there is a documented home energy emergency. Most program descriptions frame that emergency around a past due bill, a shut off notice, or being out of fuel, so a household whose equipment has failed should describe the situation and any health impact clearly when they call. The local agency makes the determination.

Benefit amounts, and how many benefits a household can receive per season, are set by FloridaCommerce and vary by region and by available funding. Ask the local agency what applies in your loved one's county rather than planning around a figure you read elsewhere.

faqs.answer: It may be. The program's described uses include repairs and replacement of existing cooling equipment, so failed equipment is within what EHEAP can address. Most official descriptions frame the qualifying emergency around a past due bill or a shut off notice, so the local agency makes the call. When you phone, state plainly that the cooling is not working and describe any medical condition the heat is affecting, so the health impact is on the record.

faqs.question: How is EHEAP different from LIHEAP?
faqs.answer: LIHEAP is the broader energy assistance program open to low-income households of any age, and it pays toward the utility bill. EHEAP is for households with someone 60 or older who are in an energy emergency, and it can go beyond the bill to repair or replace heating and cooling equipment. They are separate applications and run through different agencies, so a household may be able to use both.

faqs.question: Who actually takes the application?
faqs.answer: The Area Agency on Aging or the Aging and Disability Resource Center serving the county, sometimes through a local senior services partner. Calling the statewide Elder Helpline at 1-800-963-5337 is the reliable way to reach the right one, because the provider differs by county.

faqs.question: When can my loved one apply for cooling help?
faqs.answer: The cooling season runs April 1 through September 30, and the heating season runs October 1 through March 31. A household may receive a benefit in each season, subject to the limits and funding set for the region.

faqs.question: How much will EHEAP pay?
faqs.answer: The maximum is set by FloridaCommerce and varies by region and by the funding a local agency has left. Published figures differ from county to county, so ask the local agency what applies rather than planning around a number found online.

faqs.question: Does my loved one need to own their home?
faqs.answer: No. The requirement is that the household is responsible for the home's heating or cooling costs. Renters can qualify, though work on equipment owned by a landlord may need the landlord's cooperation.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members routinely help with the call and the paperwork. Bring the household's income documentation and identification, and expect the agency to want to verify details with the person who is 60 or older.

programs.tagline: Free home energy improvements that can lower your loved one's utility bills by hundreds of dollars annually

programs.intro:
If your loved one struggles with high energy bills and their household earns less than $31,300/year for one person (200% of the federal poverty level), they may qualify for free home energy improvements through Florida's Weatherization Assistance Program. The program provides up to $2,600 in upgrades, attic insulation, energy-efficient appliances, new water heaters, heating/cooling system repairs, all at no cost.

Priority goes to households with someone 60+, people with disabilities, or families with children under 12. Funding is limited and demand is high, so most areas have waitlists. Both homeowners and renters qualify, but renters need landlord approval since the improvements stay with the property.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply if they rent their home?
faqs.answer: Yes, renters are eligible, but the landlord must provide written consent, since the energy improvements become the landlord's property at no cost. The landlord cannot pass the cost through to the tenant.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's county doesn't appear to have a local office?
faqs.answer: Every county in Florida is covered by a designated provider. If a local agency isn't listed specifically for the county, a larger regional agency (like Capital Area Community Action or Centro-Campesino Center) has been assigned to manage that area. The full 2026 regional map and contact directory is at floridacommerce.gov.

faqs.question: How long is the waitlist really?
faqs.answer: Varies by county and funding, typically 6–18 months. Households with someone 60+, disabled members, or children under 12 get priority points and move through the queue faster.

faqs.question: What are the alternatives if the waitlist is too long?
faqs.answer: Apply for LIHEAP in parallel; it helps with immediate utility bills and emergency HVAC repairs while you wait. Many utility providers (FPL, Duke Energy) also offer free energy audits and rebates that can be used alongside WAP.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes. Family members can handle the application and paperwork. The applicant must be present for the home assessment, and documentation must be in their name as the resident.

faqs.question: How are Social Security and pensions counted toward the income limit?
faqs.answer: All income sources, including Social Security retirement (SSA/SSDI) and pensions, are counted toward the 200% FPL limit ($31,300/year for one person in 2026). One exception: if the household receives SSI (Supplemental Security Income, needs-based) or TANF, they're "categorically eligible" and automatically pass the income test, though they still need to complete the standard application. Note the difference: SSI grants auto-eligibility; regular Social Security does not.

faqs.question: What if the home needs major repairs before weatherization can begin?
faqs.answer: The program focuses on energy efficiency, not structural renovation. If a home has severe issues (failing roof, active mold, unsafe electrical), the agency may "defer" the work. That's not necessarily a final no; many Florida agencies can connect you with Pre-WAP or SHIP (State Housing Initiatives Partnership) funds to address the repairs first so the home becomes weatherization-ready.

faqs.question: How do I know if someone calling about weatherization is legitimate?
faqs.answer: Legitimate WAP staff will never ask for payment, credit card numbers, or "payroll updates" over the phone. Contractors may call to schedule an audit; they'll already have your application details. If someone demands immediate home access or asks for sensitive data, hang up and call your county's official intake office (floridacommerce.gov directory) to verify.

faqs.question: Will SHINE counselors recommend specific insurance plans?
faqs.answer: No, SHINE volunteers provide unbiased information but don't recommend or sell specific plans. They'll explain your loved one's options, compare costs and coverage, but the choice remains yours. This ensures you get objective guidance without sales pressure.

faqs.question: Can SHINE help if my loved one missed Medicare enrollment deadlines?

faqs.question: Is SHINE available year-round or only during Medicare Open Enrollment?
faqs.answer: SHINE counseling is available year-round through trained volunteers. While they're busiest during Medicare Open Enrollment (October 15 - December 7), you can get help with appeals, prescription assistance, and plan questions anytime.

programs.intro:
If your loved one struggles to shop for groceries or prepare meals safely, they may qualify for home-delivered meals through local Meals on Wheels programs or their Medicaid plan. Your loved one age 60+ who is assessed as homebound or has significant difficulty preparing meals can receive hot, frozen, or special diet meals delivered directly to their door.

Many programs are free or request a small voluntary donation for qualifying low-income seniors; others charge a private-pay fee, typically $7.00 to $9.49 per meal. For enrollees in Medicaid Long-Term Care (LTC) plans, meals are provided at no cost. There is no fixed limit on the number of meals — the amount is determined by the specific health plan's medical authorization based on documented nutritional needs. Because government-funded programs are not entitlements and rely on limited funding, significant waitlists are common, so applying early is essential.

faqs.question: Can I apply for my loved one who lives in a different county than me?
faqs.answer: Yes, but your loved one must apply through the ADRC in the county where they live, not where you live. Each county operates its own program with different providers, waitlists, and eligibility requirements.

faqs.question: What if my loved one owns a car but can no longer drive safely?
faqs.answer: Car ownership alone may not disqualify them, but the local assessor will evaluate whether your loved one can realistically use the vehicle for grocery shopping. If they've stopped driving due to vision, mobility, or cognitive issues, document this with medical records.

faqs.question: How long are the waitlists really?
faqs.answer: Wait times vary dramatically by county and season. Some areas may have immediate openings while others have months-long waitlists. South Florida tends to have longer waits due to higher demand. Priority is typically given to those at highest nutritional risk.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get both Medicaid meal delivery and community Meals on Wheels?
faqs.answer: No. Your loved one cannot receive meals from both programs simultaneously. If they are eligible for Medicaid Long-Term Care (LTC) benefits, their health plan will authorize meals based on their specific clinical assessment. These authorized meals typically offer faster approval and more consistent delivery than community-based waitlists.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one moves to assisted living after starting meal delivery?
faqs.answer: Meal delivery typically stops once a senior moves into an assisted living facility (ALF), as these facilities are legally required to provide residents with daily nutrition. Medicaid LTC plans generally do not authorize home-delivered meals for those living in ALFs. If they move to an independent living community, they may still be eligible, but this must be verified with their local ADRC.

faqs.question: Can I pay for meals if my loved one doesn't qualify for free service?
faqs.answer: Many programs offer fee-for-service options at approximately $9.49 per meal for those who don't meet income requirements but still need meal delivery. Contact your local ADRC to ask about private-pay options.

faqs.question: What if my loved one has special dietary needs like diabetic or pureed meals?
faqs.answer: Most programs accommodate special diets including diabetic-friendly, low-sodium, pureed, and other medically necessary modifications. Document dietary requirements with a physician's note during the application process to ensure appropriate meal planning.

faqs.question: How quickly can meal delivery start in an emergency situation?
faqs.answer: Emergency placements may be possible for seniors being discharged from the hospital or facing immediate nutritional crisis. Contact the local ADRC immediately and mention the urgent nature, some programs reserve emergency slots for these situations.

faqs.question: Is there a limit on how many Medicaid meals my loved one can receive?
faqs.answer: No. Under a Medicaid Long-Term Care plan there is no fixed cap on the number of home-delivered meals. The quantity is authorized by your loved one's specific health plan based on their documented medical and nutritional needs, so it varies from person to person.

programs.intro: If you're caring for a loved one with memory loss, you know it's a 24/7 commitment that can leave you exhausted. Florida's ADI program is designed to give you the "backup" you need. Whether it's a trained worker coming to your home so you can run errands or secure care at a day center while you rest, this program focuses on keeping you healthy so you can keep your loved one safe at home. Best of all, there are no asset limits to qualify — only monthly income is used to determine a small co-pay.

faqs.question: What if my loved one is under 60 but has early-onset dementia?
faqs.answer: Some local Area Agencies on Aging have different age requirements, for example, Broward County serves adults 18+. Call 1-800-963-5337 to check if your region has exceptions for younger adults with dementia.

faqs.question: How much will the sliding-scale co-payment cost?
faqs.answer: Florida doesn't publish specific co-payment amounts, this is determined individually by your local AAA based on your loved one's income. During your assessment, ask for the co-payment schedule so you can budget accordingly.

faqs.question: Can I get emergency respite if I haven't used regular respite services?
faqs.answer: Yes, emergency respite is available for crisis situations even if you're not enrolled in ongoing respite. Call your local AAA immediately when you have a caregiver emergency, don't wait for regular intake processes.

faqs.question: What's the difference between in-home respite and adult day care through this program?
faqs.answer: In-home respite brings a trained worker to your loved one's home while you take a break. Adult day care means taking your loved one to a facility with activities and supervision. Both are covered, and your AAA can help you choose based on your loved one's needs and preferences.

faqs.question: What if there's no funding available in my area right now?
faqs.answer: Ask your AAA when funding typically becomes available again and request to be put on a waiting list. Also ask about emergency respite, which may have separate funding, and other programs through the same agency that might help.

faqs.question: Can I apply for this program and Medicaid waiver services at the same time?
faqs.answer: No. ADI is a state-funded program specifically for people who are not currently enrolled in the Statewide Medicaid Managed Care Long-Term Care (LTC) program. If your loved one is approved for the Medicaid LTC waiver, they will transition to that program for their respite care, and their ADI services will end to prevent a duplication of benefits.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's dementia progresses and they need more care?
faqs.answer: Your AAA will reassess your loved one's needs regularly and can adjust services accordingly. The program specifically serves people at risk of nursing home placement, so they understand progressive conditions and can help you plan next steps.

faqs.question: Do respite workers have special training for dementia care?
faqs.answer: Workers should have training in dementia care, but training requirements vary by provider. Ask your AAA about the qualifications and training of respite workers in your area, and request workers experienced with your loved one's specific behaviors or needs.

programs.tagline: If your loved one is 55+ and unemployed with low income, they can earn minimum wage while training for permanent jobs.

localEntities.name: National Caucus and Center on Black Aged (NCBA)

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 55 or older, unemployed, and struggling to find work, SCSEP provides paid job training at nonprofits and government agencies. Your loved one earns minimum wage for an average of 20 hours per week while learning new skills at places like schools, libraries, or senior centers. While the program focuses on helping participants find permanent, unsubsidized employment as soon as they are ready, individuals may participate for up to 48 months over their lifetime.

To qualify, your loved one's household income must be at or below 125% of the federal poverty level and they must have poor employment prospects. Priority goes to veterans, people over 65, those with disabilities, low literacy, limited English proficiency, rural residents, or those experiencing homelessness. Because this is a federal program with limited funding, there may be waiting periods depending on your area.

SCSEP operates statewide in Florida through multiple organizations including the Florida Department of Elder Affairs, AARP Foundation, and other community partners. Each area offers different types of training positions based on local needs and available host sites.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply if they're already receiving Social Security or unemployment benefits?
faqs.answer: Yes, your loved one can receive Social Security and still qualify for SCSEP as long as their total household income stays at or below 125% of the federal poverty level. Unemployment benefits also count toward income but don't disqualify them if they're still within the income limits.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one doesn't find permanent work after the 6-month training period?
faqs.answer: SCSEP is a bridge to permanent work, and while many find jobs quickly, participants can remain in the program for up to 48 months over their lifetime to gain the necessary skills. Job placement assistance is provided throughout the entire time they are enrolled.

faqs.question: How long is the wait to get into the program?
faqs.answer: Wait times vary significantly by region and depend on federal funding availability. Priority applicants (veterans, those 65+, people with disabilities) typically get placed first. Contact your local provider directly for current availability in your area.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one who has difficulty making phone calls?
faqs.answer: Most SCSEP providers allow family members to help with the initial inquiry and application process, but your loved one will likely need to complete the interview and assessment personally since this is an employment program requiring their direct participation.

faqs.question: What types of jobs will my loved one be trained for?
faqs.answer: Training positions are typically at nonprofits, schools, hospitals, senior centers, and government agencies. Common roles include clerical aide, teacher's assistant, receptionist, or support staff. The specific positions available depend on host sites in your local area.

faqs.question: Can my loved one participate in SCSEP and look for other jobs at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, SCSEP encourages participants to actively search for permanent employment while in the program. The goal is to transition to unsubsidized work as quickly as possible, and job search assistance is part of the program services.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income changes during the program?
faqs.answer: SCSEP providers typically reassess eligibility periodically. If your loved one's income rises above 125% of the poverty level due to other income sources, they may no longer be eligible to continue in the program but should still receive job placement assistance.

faqs.question: Does my loved one need previous work experience to qualify?
faqs.answer: No specific work experience is required, and the program actually prioritizes people with poor employment prospects, which can include those with limited work history, long-term unemployment, or outdated skills. The training is designed to build employable skills regardless of background.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is too high for some programs but they still need help?

faqs.question: Will they represent my loved one in court or just give advice?

programs.name: Home Care for the Elderly (HCE) Program
programs.tagline: A monthly financial subsidy paid to a live-in family caregiver to help keep your loved one out of a nursing home.

localEntities.name: Local Aging and Disability Resource Centers (ADRCs), DOEA contractors

programs.intro:
Florida's HCE Program recognizes that family members are often the best caregivers, but that the costs of caring for a senior can add up quickly. Rather than sending a stranger into your home, this program provides you — the live-in caregiver — with a monthly check (starting at $160) to help cover the costs of food, medical supplies, and basic needs. It's a way for the state to support the incredible work you're already doing to keep your loved one out of a nursing home.

To qualify in 2026, the senior must meet specific clinical and financial criteria. Clinically, they must be certified as needing a Nursing Home Level of Care, and they must live in a private home with a caregiver who is willing and able to provide or coordinate their care. Financially, the senior's gross monthly income must be under $2,982, and their countable assets must be under $2,000 for an individual or $3,000 for a couple. All participants receive a basic monthly subsidy of $160, and additional special subsidies may be authorized for medical supplies, home health aide services, or nutritional supplements.

Because HCE is a state-funded program and not an entitlement, most areas use a Statewide Pre-Enrollment List (Apply early!). Unlike standard waitlists, placement on this list is determined by the senior's frailty and risk score rather than the date of their application. To begin the process and determine if your loved one qualifies for a full assessment, call the statewide Elder Helpline at 1-800-963-5337 for a preliminary phone screening.

faqs.question: Can my loved one qualify if they own their home worth more than $2,000?
faqs.answer: Yes, the primary residence is typically exempt from asset limits under Medicaid ICP rules. However, there may be home equity caps that apply. The $2,000 limit refers to countable assets like bank accounts, investments, and additional vehicles.

faqs.question: What if our family member can't be the live-in caregiver full-time?
faqs.answer: The caregiver must live in the home but doesn't have to provide all care personally. They need to coordinate services and be available to assist, but can arrange for additional help. They must pass the assessment showing they're willing and able to manage the care arrangement.

faqs.question: How long is the waitlist really?
faqs.answer: The program doesn't publish waitlist times, and it varies significantly by region and priority level. Those at highest risk of immediate nursing home placement get priority. Contact your local ADRC for current availability in your specific area.

faqs.question: Can I apply for this program and Medicaid Long-Term Care at the same time?
faqs.answer: No. Your loved one cannot be enrolled in HCE if they are already receiving services through Florida's Statewide Medicaid Managed Care (SMMC) Long-Term Care program. HCE is intended to provide a financial bridge for caregivers supporting seniors who meet clinical requirements but are not yet receiving comprehensive Medicaid managed care services.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's needs increase after enrollment?
faqs.answer: The case manager will reassess your loved one's condition and adjust services accordingly. If needs exceed what can be safely provided at home even with HCE support, transition planning to higher levels of care may be necessary.

faqs.question: Does the live-in caregiver get paid through this program?
faqs.answer: The program provides support services to help the caregiver arrangement work, but it's not primarily a paid caregiver program. The focus is on preventing nursing home placement through family-based care with professional support services.

faqs.question: What if my loved one doesn't meet the nursing home level of care in the 701B assessment?
faqs.answer: If your loved one doesn't qualify for nursing home level care, they won't be eligible for HCE. However, they may qualify for other home and community services through Older Americans Act programs or lower-level Medicaid waiver services.

faqs.question: Can we get services immediately in a crisis situation?
faqs.answer: The program doesn't specify emergency processing times. If your loved one is being discharged from a hospital or facing immediate nursing home placement, contact your local ADRC immediately to discuss expedited assessment options.

programs.name: Community Care for the Elderly (CCE) Program
programs.tagline: Home care services, free or low cost based on income, to help your loved one age in place instead of moving to a nursing home.
programs.intro:
If your loved one is 60+ and struggling with daily tasks like bathing or medication management, Florida's Community Care for the Elderly (CCE) Program provides home care services to help them stay in their own home. The program serves as an alternative to nursing home placement by offering community-based care for seniors at risk of institutionalization.

CCE prioritizes those most at risk of needing nursing home care due to functional impairments. Because this is a state-funded program with limited capacity, there are often waiting lists for services. Eligibility is determined through a comprehensive assessment of functional needs; unlike standard entitlement programs, CCE charges a sliding co-payment on income above the federal poverty level. At or below it, services are free.

The program operates statewide through the Florida Department of Elder Affairs, but your loved one cannot receive CCE services while enrolled in a Medicaid capitated long-term care program. To start, call the Elder Helpline at 1-800-963-5337. A screener asks a few questions by phone. No paperwork is needed for that call.

contentSections.content: CCE participants cannot simultaneously receive Medicaid capitated long-term care services. If your loved one qualifies for both, you'll need to choose which program better meets their needs. This restriction is strictly enforced.

faqs.question: Can my loved one receive both CCE and Medicaid long-term care services?
faqs.answer: No. Florida prohibits dual enrollment in CCE and Medicaid capitated long-term care programs. You must choose one program. If your loved one qualifies for both, compare the services offered to determine which better meets their needs.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one misses their annual reassessment?
faqs.answer: Missing the annual comprehensive assessment can result in loss of CCE services. The reassessment is mandatory to verify continued eligibility. Contact your case manager at the lead agency immediately if you've missed an appointment to reschedule.

faqs.question: How do they determine if my loved one is 'at risk of institutionalization'?
faqs.answer: The phone screener uses the shorter 701S form first. Later a case manager performs a full functional assessment (the 701B form) to calculate a frailty score. They evaluate your loved one's ability to perform Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) such as bathing, dressing, eating, and transferring (e.g., getting out of bed), as well as memory issues or cognitive impairments like Alzheimer's.

faqs.question: What if my loved one doesn't qualify for CCE services?
faqs.answer: If your loved one clearly does not qualify, the intake worker must explain the rules and refer you to other help when appropriate. Ask specifically about this referral process and what other programs might be available.

faqs.question: Can I apply for CCE while my loved one is in the hospital?
faqs.answer: Yes. If your loved one is hospitalized, notify the hospital social worker and call the Elder Helpline immediately. While CCE cannot provide services inside the hospital, early screening can help prioritize them for the Statewide Pre-Enrollment List to facilitate a safer discharge back home.

faqs.question: How long is the waitlist for CCE services?
faqs.answer: CCE uses a Statewide Pre-Enrollment List. Because placement is based on a priority score (frailty) rather than the date you applied, wait times are unpredictable. A senior with high medical needs may be moved to the top of the list within weeks; a more independent senior may wait significantly longer. Call the Elder Helpline at 1-800-963-5337 for a screening to see where your loved one ranks.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes. Family members or caregivers can initiate the process via the Elder Helpline. To sign official state documents or make medical/financial decisions during the assessment, you will typically need a Florida Durable Power of Attorney (DPOA) or to be a designated Health Care Surrogate.

faqs.question: What specific services does CCE provide?
faqs.answer: CCE covers a range of community-based services, including in-home support (homemaking, personal care, meals), medical care (nursing, therapy, supplies), support services (adult day care, emergency alert systems, home repairs), and caregiver relief through respite care.

This program offers personalized home and community-based services including personal care assistance, homemaker services, adult day care, and caregiver respite, all designed as alternatives to institutionalization.

Because Elder Options tailors services to each person's specific needs after a comprehensive assessment, there are no fixed dollar amounts or guaranteed hours. Your loved one must meet both financial eligibility (following Florida Medicaid rules) and medical eligibility through a Nursing Facility Level of Care assessment that determines they need daily help with activities of daily living. Income limits for 2026: $2,982/month for a single person applying for nursing home-level services.

faqs.answer: Yes, the primary home is exempt from asset limits up to $752,000 in equity if your loved one lives there or intends to return. The $2,000 asset limit applies to countable assets like bank accounts, investments, and second properties, not the primary residence. If a spouse or dependent child still lives in the home, the equity cap is waived entirely.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one lives outside the Elder Options service area?
faqs.answer: Elder Options serves 16 counties in North Central Florida (Alachua, Bradford, Citrus, Columbia, Dixie, Gilchrist, Hamilton, Hernando, Lafayette, Lake, Levy, Marion, Putnam, Sumter, Suwannee, and Union). If your loved one lives elsewhere in Florida, call the statewide Elder Helpline at 1-800-963-5337 to be routed to the correct local ADRC.

faqs.question: How long is the waitlist really?
faqs.answer: Waitlist times vary significantly by service type and funding availability in your specific area. Some services may be available immediately while others could have months-long waits. Ask Elder Options staff for current wait times for the specific services your loved one needs when you call.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can initiate the application process, but your loved one will need to participate in the CARES assessment and provide consent for services. If your loved one has cognitive impairment, you may need legal documentation like power of attorney to complete the full process.

faqs.question: What if my loved one doesn't qualify for Nursing Facility Level of Care?
faqs.answer: If the CARES assessment determines your loved one doesn't need nursing home-level care, they won't qualify for most long-term care services through Elder Options. However, they may still be eligible for other programs or services, Elder Options staff can provide referrals to appropriate alternatives.

faqs.question: Can my loved one receive Elder Options services and keep their Medicare Advantage plan?
faqs.answer: This depends on the specific services and your loved one's current coverage. Some Elder Options programs work alongside Medicare Advantage while others may require enrollment in specific Medicaid managed care plans. Discuss this with Elder Options staff during the application process.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's needs change after they start receiving services?
faqs.answer: Elder Options conducts periodic reassessments to adjust services based on changing needs. If your loved one's condition improves or worsens, contact Elder Options to request a reassessment and potential service plan modification.

faqs.question: Is there a co-payment required for Elder Options services?
faqs.answer: Some programs may require co-payments or have means testing even after Medicaid eligibility is established. The amount depends on your loved one's income and the specific services received. This will be explained during the service planning process if applicable.

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65 or older or has a disability, MEDS-AD is the Florida Medicaid pathway that may provide full medical coverage when income and assets are very limited. It is different from SMMC-LTC: MEDS-AD is regular SSI-related Medicaid coverage, while SMMC-LTC adds long-term care services after a separate level-of-care process.

For April 2026 standards, Florida lists MEDS-AD income limits of $1,171/month for one person and $1,588/month for a couple. The asset limits are $5,000 for one person and $6,000 for a couple. People who already receive SSI are automatically eligible for Medicaid and usually do not need a separate ACCESS Florida application unless nursing home or waiver services are needed.

The cleanest starting point is the MyACCESS application. If your loved one needs home and community-based services or nursing home care, the DCF Medicaid page says to check the HCBS/Waivers or Nursing Home option during the application so the case is routed for the right long-term care review.

faqs.answer: No. MEDS-AD is a Medicaid coverage group for low-income people who are 65 or older or disabled. SMMC-LTC is the long-term care managed care program that can pay for home and community-based services after a separate level-of-care process.

faqs.question: What are the April 2026 MEDS-AD limits?
faqs.answer: Florida's April 2026 SSI-related financial chart lists MEDS-AD limits of $1,171/month income and $5,000 assets for one person. For a couple, the listed limits are $1,588/month income and $6,000 assets.

faqs.question: Does my parent need to apply if they already receive SSI?

faqs.question: What if my loved one needs home care, not just a Medicaid card?

faqs.question: How long does DCF take to decide?

faqs.question: Can a caregiver apply on behalf of an older parent?

programs.intro:
If your loved one lives in a nursing home, assisted living facility, adult family care home, or continuing care retirement community, Florida's Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program can help when something feels wrong. Ombudsmen investigate complaints, explain resident rights, and advocate for quality of life and care.

This is not Medicaid and it does not pay for care. It is a free, confidential advocacy program focused on residents of long-term care facilities. Florida says the program works through 14 district offices that cover the state, with volunteers and staff investigating and resolving complaints made by or on behalf of residents.

Call 1-888-831-0404 when you need help with facility discharge threats, care concerns, rights violations, communication problems, or unresolved complaints.

programs.intro:
If you are caring for an older parent at home, Florida's National Family Caregiver Support Program can connect you with services that reduce the pressure on the caregiver, not just the person receiving care. Services may include information, help getting access to services, counseling, support groups, caregiver training, respite care, transportation, material aid, legal assistance, and supplemental services.

Florida administers the program through Title III-E of the federal Older Americans Act. Funds go to Area Agencies on Aging, which contract with local providers, so the exact services and availability depend on your region.

The program can serve adult family members caring for someone age 60 or older. It can also serve grandparents or other relatives age 55 or older who care for children 18 or younger, or children of any age who have disabilities.

stateOverview.intro: Florida offers 13 programs to help your aging loved one stay home safely and afford basic needs. These range from monthly financial benefits (like $400–$2,000 toward utility bills through LIHEAP) to free services (like home-delivered meals and legal aid). Most programs focus on in-home care alternatives to nursing home placement, Florida has multiple waiver programs and home care services designed to keep seniors aging in place. Start by checking if your loved one qualifies for Medicaid home care waivers or Medicare assistance programs, as these provide the most comprehensive financial relief. For immediate help navigating options, SHINE offers free one-on-one guidance for any Florida senior.

quickFacts: Florida has five separate programs offering in-home care alternatives to nursing home placement, most require Medicaid eligibility or specific income limits.
SHINE provides free Medicare counseling to every Florida senior regardless of income, call 1-800-963-5337.
Most income-based programs use limits around $2,000–$2,600/month for a single person, but each has different requirements.
Area Agencies on Aging manage many local programs, your loved one's specific services depend on which of Florida's 11 regions they live in.
stateOverview.resourcesVsBenefits: Florida programs fall into two categories: qualification-based benefits that require meeting income or health criteria (like Medicaid waivers or LIHEAP utility assistance), and free resources available to all seniors (like SHINE Medicare counseling or legal aid through Area Agencies on Aging). Start with the free resources, SHINE can help determine which benefits your loved one might qualify for, and legal aid can assist with applications or appeals.
